meta.title: Who really said "Smart people learn from everything and everyone"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Socrates. It appears in none of the four sources that transmit him — Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes, Diogenes Laërtius — and no source of any kind has ever been produced for it. It is a modern motivational line with an unknown author.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Smart people learn from everything and everyone'?
meta.ogDescription: No ancient source, no modern one either. Socrates wrote nothing, and this is in none of the four writers who transmit him. Author: genuinely unknown.

answer.label: Not Socrates — a modern saying, author unknown
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · modern — no source of any kind located
answer.sourceLine: Socrates wrote nothing down, so anything of his has to come through Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Diogenes Laërtius. This line is in none of them, in any translation. It also does not read like a translation from Greek: it is a three-part motivational structure — smart / average / stupid — of a kind that belongs to modern business writing, not to a fourth-century BC Athenian. We could not find a first appearance, an author, or even a date. What we can say for certain is what it is not.
answer.confidenceText: No ancient source. No modern source either. Just a very shareable sentence.

None — absent from Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and Diogenes Laërtius

source.excerpt: But I observed that even the good artisans fell into the same error as the poets;—because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters, and this defect in them overshadowed their wisdom.
trail: The decisive test is short. Socrates wrote nothing, so there are exactly four places a genuine Socrates line can live — Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes, Diogenes Laërtius. This sentence is in none of them.

Nor is there a modern trail. Unlike the better-known fakes, nobody has produced a first printing, a misattributing newspaper or a self-help book to blame. It surfaces in quotation aggregators and on social media already wearing the Socrates label, with no citation attached — which is the signature of a line invented for the internet rather than lifted from a book.

We are stating the absence rather than filling it. ‘No source located’ is an honest finding; inventing a Greek reference to make the page look complete would be exactly the error this site exists to correct.
source.excerptNote: The genuine Socratic version of the same idea, from Jowett’s Plato. Notice how much less flattering it is to the reader. Socrates is not sorting people into smart, average and stupid; he is saying that real expertise is precisely what tempts a person to think they know everything else — a warning aimed at competent people, not at fools.
source.rightsNote: The excerpt above is Benjamin Jowett’s nineteenth-century translation of Plato’s Apology, long out of copyright and free to reproduce. The disputed sentence at the top of this page is a different matter: with no identified author and no known date of first publication, its copyright status cannot be determined, so we make no claim about it. Attribute it as anonymous and modern. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Socrates
author.bio: Socrates spent his life arguing that he knew nothing and that the people most certain of their knowledge were the ones worth questioning — which makes him a magnet for any line about clever people, dim people and the gap between them. The trouble is that he left no writings, so there is no corpus to check a claim against, only four other men’s accounts of him. That absence is what makes him the single most convenient name in the language to hang an invented aphorism on.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a widely shared fake Socrates line, and it is also one of the emptiest — there is nothing behind it at all, in either direction.

items.why: He wrote nothing, so it would have to be in Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Diogenes Laërtius. It is in none of them, in any wording. No fragment, no ancient testimony, nothing.

Unusually, there is no culprit to name either. No first printing, no misquoting newspaper, no self-help bestseller. It appears fully formed in quotation databases and social posts, already labelled Socrates.

Smart / average / stupid is a management-seminar cadence. Greek philosophical writing, and the translations of it, do not sort humanity into a tidy tricolon of flattery, mild insult and hard insult — and the ranking rewards the reader, who is invited to place themselves in the first group.

Socrates really did argue that certainty is the enemy of learning — but the version in Plato aims the warning at skilled, competent people who overreach, not at ‘stupid people.’ The fake keeps the shape of the thought and loses the sting.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous modern saying. No source of any kind has been produced, and it appears in none of the four writers through whom Socrates survives.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It works because it hands the reader a compliment and a target in the same breath. You are obviously in the first group, learning from everything and everyone; the person who annoyed you this morning is obviously in the third. Very few sentences do that much social work in twenty words.

The Socrates label is doing the rest. Attach a modern motivational line to a man executed for asking awkward questions and it stops being an opinion and becomes an authority, which is precisely the move Socrates spent his life dismantling.
context.detailsSummary: What Socrates actually argued about knowing
detailsBody: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates explains the oracle’s verdict that no one is wiser than he is, and concludes that he is wiser only in knowing that he does not know.
He tests the politicians, the poets and the craftsmen in turn. The craftsmen come off best — they genuinely know their trade.
But that competence is exactly what ruins them: because they are good workmen, they assume they also understand ‘all sorts of high matters.’
The warning is therefore about experts, not idiots. It is aimed at the reader, not at somebody else.
That is the reversal the modern version quietly drops.
context.pull: Socrates aimed the warning at competent people. The fake aims it at somebody else.
